items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I think in 1926 I played with Duke Ellington for two weeks . . . They needed a saxophone player, and Duke contacted me.

ctx.x: We’ll, of course, discuss Fletcher Henderson, who you had a couple of stints with earlier, I think.

Actually, I think I had had one. I was playing with Billy Fowler’s Orchestra at a club downtown. If I remember correctly, Donald Redmond’s father died, and he had to go back to Piedmont, West Virginia, or Virginia, wherever Piedmont is, and Fletcher asked me if I could come and work in . . . substitute for Don Redmond while he was gone. So I think I asked Billy Fowler, or maybe Fletcher approached him directly, I’m not sure. But Billy said sure, it was okay. He allowed me to do it. And because it was really…

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: I sat in for Harvey Boon for a week or two ... playing with the great Ellington

ctx.x: The name ... you had given permission for the name to be used, or did it sort of refer to you?

Well, that's a very strange thing, because at this moment, I can't recall -- maybe they may have even felt ... when I say 'they' I mean the Mills organization, -- they may have felt that they owned the name as they owned Baron Lee. Duke Ellington was, of course, Duke Ellington's name, Earl Hines was his name -- so they wouldn't have owned that. But King Carter was not necessarily my name, nor was it a name that I went by as a nickname at that time.
And they recorded -- that the King Carter group recorded "Blues in My Heart".

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: I was just wondering what kind of music it was that you and the Fletcher Hendersons or the Don Redmonds or the Duke Ellingtons would have been listening to and impressed by.

ctx.x: 'Happy' Caldwells, and Tommy Ladnier, Fletcher Henderson from Cuthbert, Cutpit, Georgia, yes. And gee whiz, it's -- you know -- it was also the melting pot of jazz, you know? New York was ... because of so many musicians from other parts of the country.

Well, one thing struck me in reading Stanley Dance's book which recently came out, which was that a number of musicians who were based in New York described it -- it was much later in their careers when they heard what was described as "Dixieland" music, whatever it is that they mean by Dixieland music, and I was just wondering what kind of music it was that you and the Fletcher Hendersons or the Don Redmonds or the Duke Ellingtons would have been listening to and impressed by. You mentioned Frankie Trumbauer…

Yes, Frankie Trombar, and I didn't -- I wasn't impressed by too much else of the orchestra with which he was playing. I remember he was playing with the Benson orchestra of Chicago, and the record that I did like of his that I think I even heard before I heard "Singin' The Blues" -- now chronologically, I may be wrong about this, but I think I heard "I'll Never Miss the Sunshine; I'm So Used to the Rain" ...
